claim: The pupil provides a rich, non-invasive measure of the neural bases of perception and cognition.
source: The pupil provides a rich, non-invasive measure of the neural bases of perception and cognition and has been of particular value in uncovering the role of arousal-linked neuromodulation, which alters both cortical processing and pupil size.
evidence: This is a general statement about pupillometry that draws from established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: The pupil has been of particular value in uncovering the role of arousal-linked neuromodulation.
source: The pupil provides a rich, non-invasive measure of the neural bases of perception and cognition and has been of particular value in uncovering the role of arousal-linked neuromodulation, which alters both cortical processing and pupil size.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about the utility of pupillometry in studying neuromodulation.

claim: Arousal-linked neuromodulation alters both cortical processing and pupil size.
source: The pupil provides a rich, non-invasive measure of the neural bases of perception and cognition and has been of particular value in uncovering the role of arousal-linked neuromodulation, which alters both cortical processing and pupil size.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about neuromodulation effects.

claim: Perceptual changes during multistability were marked by a complex pupil response that could be decomposed into two components.
source: Perceptual changes were marked by a complex pupil response that could be decomposed into two components: a dilation tied to task execution and plausibly indicative of an arousal-linked noradrenaline surge, and an overlapping constriction tied to the perceptual transient and plausibly a marker of altered visual cortical representation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: One component of the pupil response is a dilation tied to task execution.
source: Perceptual changes were marked by a complex pupil response that could be decomposed into two components: a dilation tied to task execution and plausibly indicative of an arousal-linked noradrenaline surge, and an overlapping constriction tied to the perceptual transient and plausibly a marker of altered visual cortical representation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data, specifically from comparing Report and Ignore conditions.

claim: The task-related dilation component is plausibly indicative of an arousal-linked noradrenaline surge.
source: Perceptual changes were marked by a complex pupil response that could be decomposed into two components: a dilation tied to task execution and plausibly indicative of an arousal-linked noradrenaline surge, and an overlapping constriction tied to the perceptual transient and plausibly a marker of altered visual cortical representation.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on inference from the data and established knowledge about pupil dilation and noradrenaline.

claim: One component of the pupil response is a constriction tied to the perceptual transient.
source: Perceptual changes were marked by a complex pupil response that could be decomposed into two components: a dilation tied to task execution and plausibly indicative of an arousal-linked noradrenaline surge, and an overlapping constriction tied to the perceptual transient and plausibly a marker of altered visual cortical representation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data, particularly from the Ignore conditions.

claim: The perception-related constriction is plausibly a marker of altered visual cortical representation.
source: Perceptual changes were marked by a complex pupil response that could be decomposed into two components: a dilation tied to task execution and plausibly indicative of an arousal-linked noradrenaline surge, and an overlapping constriction tied to the perceptual transient and plausibly a marker of altered visual cortical representation.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on inference from the data and established knowledge about pupil constriction to isoluminant changes.

claim: Constriction amplitude systematically depended on the time interval between perceptual changes.
source: Constriction, but not dilation, amplitude systematically depended on the time interval between perceptual changes, possibly providing an overt index of neural adaptation.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Dilation amplitude did not systematically depend on the time interval between perceptual changes.
source: Constriction, but not dilation, amplitude systematically depended on the time interval between perceptual changes, possibly providing an overt index of neural adaptation.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The dependence of constriction on time interval between perceptual changes possibly provides an overt index of neural adaptation.
source: Constriction, but not dilation, amplitude systematically depended on the time interval between perceptual changes, possibly providing an overt index of neural adaptation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed data pattern.

claim: The pupil provides a simultaneous reading on interacting but dissociable neural processes during perceptual multistability.
source: These results show that the pupil provides a simultaneous reading on interacting but dissociable neural processes during perceptual multistability, and suggest that arousal-linked neuromodulator release shapes action but not perception in these circumstances.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings showing two separable pupil components.

claim: Arousal-linked neuromodulator release shapes action but not perception during perceptual multistability.
source: These results show that the pupil provides a simultaneous reading on interacting but dissociable neural processes during perceptual multistability, and suggest that arousal-linked neuromodulator release shapes action but not perception in these circumstances.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the finding that task-related dilation (linked to noradrenaline) is associated with action, while perception-related constriction is not.

claim: The brainstem's neuromodulatory systems can profoundly influence cognitive functions by altering neural response properties within cortical circuits.
source: The brainstem's neuromodulatory systems can profoundly influence cognitive functions by altering neural response properties within the cortical circuits that mediate those functions (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Sara and Bouret, 2012; Lee and Dan, 2012; Pfeffer et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The noradrenergic arousal system associated with the brainstem's locus coeruleus impacts perception during multistable vision.
source: recent work suggests that the noradrenergic arousal system associated with the brainstem's locus coeruleus impacts perception in this situation, perhaps by altering the response gain of visual cortical neurons involved (Einhäuser et al., 2008; Sara and Bouret, 2012; Laeng et al., 2012; Kloosterman et al., 2015a; Pfeffer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The noradrenergic arousal system may impact perception during multistable vision by altering the response gain of visual cortical neurons.
source: recent work suggests that the noradrenergic arousal system associated with the brainstem's locus coeruleus impacts perception in this situation, perhaps by altering the response gain of visual cortical neurons involved (Einhäuser et al., 2008; Sara and Bouret, 2012; Laeng et al., 2012; Kloosterman et al., 2015a; Pfeffer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Pupil dilations can non-invasively convey noradrenaline release.
source: Like previous researchers, we focused on pupil size changes that accompany switches between alternative percepts, because pupil dilations can non-invasively convey noradrenaline release (Murphy et al., 2014; Joshi et al., 2016; de Gee et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Existing results reveal a transient pupil dilation accompanying perceptual switches during multistable perception.
source: Existing results reveal a transient pupil dilation accompanying perceptual switches, suggestive of a noradrenaline surge (Einhäuser et al., 2008; Hupé et al., 2009; Kloosterman et al., 2015b; de Hollander et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The transient pupil dilation accompanying perceptual switches is suggestive of a noradrenaline surge.
source: Existing results reveal a transient pupil dilation accompanying perceptual switches, suggestive of a noradrenaline surge (Einhäuser et al., 2008; Hupé et al., 2009; Kloosterman et al., 2015b; de Hollander et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an interpretation from prior research supported by citations.

claim: Perceptual switches in existing work always involved multiple neural events spaced closely in time.
source: But what complicates interpretation of the published results is that perceptual switches always involved multiple neural events spaced closely in time—some related to perception and some not—which makes it difficult to tie pupillary measures back to any specific event (see Hupé et al., 2009 for a similar assessment).
evidence: This is an assessment of prior research supported by a citation.

claim: Perceptual switches in existing work were always task relevant.
source: In particular, perceptual switches in existing work were always task relevant—observers overtly reported them or, in some cases, covertly tracked them—so that each switch included both the perceptual change and further task-related processing.
evidence: This is an assessment of the methodology used in prior research.

claim: Noradrenaline-related pupil dilations have been linked to motor planning, attentional reorienting, altered cognitive load, and surprise.
source: Of note, noradrenaline-related pupil dilations have been linked to numerous cognitive factors that may be at play in such a situation: motor planning, attentional reorienting, altered cognitive load, and surprise, among others (Kahneman and Beatty, 1966; Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Hupé et al., 2009; Laeng et al., 2012; de Gee et al., 2014; Wang and Munoz, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Binocular rivalry is a form of multistability in which perception alternates between two interpretations that each correspond to a stimulus shown to only one of the two eyes.
source: We used binocular rivalry, a form of multistability in which perception alternates between two interpretations that each correspond to a stimulus shown to only one of the two eyes (Blake and Logothetis, 2002).
evidence: This is a definition supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The direction of reflexive eye movements in response to visual motion (optokinetic nystagmus, or OKN) forms a reliable indicator of perceived motion direction during binocular rivalry.
source: Previous work has shown the direction of reflexive eye movements in response to visual motion (optokinetic nystagmus, or OKN) to form a reliable indicator of perceived motion direction in similar situations, not just for binocularly congruent motion but also during binocular rivalry (Fox et al., 1975; Leopold et al., 2001; Naber et al., 2011; Frässle et al., 2014; Aleshin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Per-observer estimates of perceptual switch rate were highly correlated between OKN-based measure and measures based on manual report or on-screen switch timing.
source: Per-observer estimates of perceptual switch rate were highly correlated (see figure caption) although not identical (see Discussion) between our OKN-based measure and measures based on either manual report or, in the On-screen conditions, replayed direction reversals (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 1C, with Pearson's r values of 0.75, 0.89, and 0.92 (all p<0.0001).

claim: There was a tight temporal correspondence between the moments of perceptual switching as identified by OKN, manual report, and on-screen switch events.
source: Moreover, there was a tight temporal correspondence between the moments of perceptual switching as identified by the three different methods (Figure 1D–E), providing further confidence in our OKN method's suitability.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis shown in Figures 1D-E.

claim: The findings on switch-related pupil responses did not importantly depend on which color or which eye became dominant during the switch.
source: We verified that our findings on switch-related pupil responses did not importantly depend on which color, or which eye, became dominant during the switch (Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: This is a control analysis result shown in Appendix 1—figure 2.

claim: Control analyses rule out the possibility that observations are importantly related to the association between perceptual switches and ocular events.
source: While, in general, changes in gaze direction can be associated with changes in pupil size, both real and apparent when using video-based eye trackers (Gagl et al., 2011; Wang and Munoz, 2015; Knapen et al., 2016; Laeng and Alnaes, 2019), control analyses rule out the possibility that our observations are importantly related to the association between perceptual switches and ocular events in our paradigm (Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: This is a control analysis result shown in Appendix 1—figure 3.

claim: Pupil response patterns were highly similar irrespective of the switch index used (OKN-based, manually reported, or on-screen).
source: To address the possible concern that our results may be impacted in a relevant way by limitations in the OKN-based switch detection algorithm, we furthermore compared results across different switch indices (OKN-based, manually reported, and on-screen) within the specific conditions that allow such comparisons, and found that pupil response patterns were highly similar irrespective of the switch index used (Appendix 1—figure 5).
evidence: This is a control analysis result shown in Appendix 1—figure 5.

claim: For both Ignore conditions, perceptual switches are accompanied by a rapid drop in pupil size followed by a rapid recovery back to near baseline.
source: For both of the Ignore conditions perceptual switches are accompanied by a rapid drop in pupil size (marked in Figure 2A as 'C1', for 'constriction 1'), followed by a rapid recovery back to near baseline ('D1', for 'dilation 1'.
evidence: This is a finding from the data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: For both Report conditions, the pupil response is more complex than in Ignore conditions.
source: For both Report conditions, on the other hand, visual inspection suggests a more complex pupil response.
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In Report conditions, the initial constriction is small enough for the re-dilation to go well past baseline, leading to a final, more gradual constriction back to near baseline later.
source: Although the initial constriction/re-dilation sequence (marked in the plots) is visible, the amplitude of the initial constriction is small enough for the re-dilation to go well past baseline, leading to a final, more gradual constriction back to near baseline later ('C2', for 'constriction 2').
evidence: This is a finding from the data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The added complexity in Report conditions is consistent with the fact that these conditions include an additional event (the key press report) on top of the perceptual change.
source: Such added complexity would be consistent with the fact that the Report conditions include an additional event, the key press report, on top of the perceptual change that these conditions share with the Ignore conditions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data pattern observed in Figure 2.

claim: The data from the Ignore conditions differ significantly from those from the Report conditions throughout most of the first three seconds following the switch event.
source: The ANOVA results (Figure 2B; center) indicate that the data from the Ignore conditions differ significantly from those from the Report conditions throughout most of the first three seconds following the switch event, overlapping with both the initial constriction and the subsequent dilation.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the ANOVA shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The initial constriction (C1) reaches significance in both Ignore conditions.
source: The figure panels themselves show that the initial constriction (C1) reaches significance in both Ignore conditions, while being visible only as a non-significant period of negative size change in the Report conditions.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The initial constriction (C1) is visible only as a non-significant period of negative size change in the Report conditions.
source: The figure panels themselves show that the initial constriction (C1) reaches significance in both Ignore conditions, while being visible only as a non-significant period of negative size change in the Report conditions.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The subsequent dilation (D1) is significant in all conditions.
source: The subsequent dilation (D1), on the other hand, is significant in all conditions.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A later period of negative size change (C2) is visible between the 2 s mark and 4 s mark for both Report conditions.
source: A later period of negative size change (C2) is visible between the 2 s mark and 4 s mark for both Report conditions, and reaches significance in the On-screen Report condition.
evidence: This is a finding from the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The later period of negative size change (C2) reaches significance in the On-screen Report condition.
source: A later period of negative size change (C2) is visible between the 2 s mark and 4 s mark for both Report conditions, and reaches significance in the On-screen Report condition.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There is a difference in pupil response between the Rivalry conditions and the On-screen conditions immediately following the switch.
source: The ANOVA results also indicate a, less extensive, difference in pupil response between the Rivalry conditions and the On-screen conditions immediately following the switch (overlapping both with the end of the initial constriction and the start of the redilation), as well as an interaction in a slightly earlier time period (overlapping mainly with the initial constriction).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the ANOVA shown in Figure 2B.

claim: On-screen switches and rivalry switches are both associated with a response of the same general shape, but the On-screen response is more rapid and pronounced.
source: A comparison between the curves of Figure 2A and between the curves of Figure 2B (left vs. right columns of plots) shows no clear qualitative difference between these two groups of conditions but, instead, suggests that on-screen switches and rivalry switches are both associated with a response of the same general shape, but that the On-screen response is more rapid and pronounced.
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: Switches in the On-screen conditions may be more abrupt than rivalry switches.
source: One possible explanation for this is that switches in the On-screen conditions may be more abrupt, which would likely make for a closer temporal alignment of switch-related pupil responses across switches, resulting in a more articulated, less smeared out, estimated pupil response.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed difference between On-screen and Rivalry conditions.

claim: For each time period examined in Figure 3, both the majority of per-observer data points and the median of those data points lie on the same side of 0 as the corresponding across-observer average.
source: In particular, for each time period examined in Figure 3, both the majority of per-observer data points and (equivalently) the median of those data points lie on the same side of 0 as the corresponding across-observer average shown in Figure 2B.
evidence: This is an observation from the per-observer data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Most individual observers numerically show a constriction/dilation whenever the across-observer average shows a significant constriction/dilation.
source: In other words, most individual observers numerically show a constriction/dilation whenever the across-observer average shows a significant constriction/dilation.
evidence: This is an observation from the per-observer data shown in Figure 3.

claim: All conditions show a similar rapid constriction (C1) and re-dilation (D1).
source: The finding that all conditions show a similar rapid constriction (C1) and re-dilation (D1) suggests that this component of the pupil response is tied to the occurrence of a (spontaneous or replayed) perceptual switch: the common factor across all conditions.
evidence: This is a finding from the data shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: The rapid constriction and re-dilation component of the pupil response is tied to the occurrence of a perceptual switch.
source: The finding that all conditions show a similar rapid constriction (C1) and re-dilation (D1) suggests that this component of the pupil response is tied to the occurrence of a (spontaneous or replayed) perceptual switch: the common factor across all conditions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data pattern observed across conditions.

claim: The onset of initial constriction closely corresponds temporally to the moment at which perception switches.
source: This suggestion is strengthened by the close temporal correspondence between the onset of initial constriction and the moment at which perception switches (the temporal reference used in Figure 2, that is the OKN-based estimate of the switch moment, typically falls within half a second of the perceptual change; see Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from the temporal analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Only the Report conditions show the re-dilation going well past baseline and being followed by a final constriction.
source: The fact that only the Report conditions show the re-dilation going well past baseline and being followed by a final constriction (significantly so for the Rivalry Report condition), suggests an additional, and later, dilation associated with manually reporting the perceptual switch.
evidence: This is a finding from the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: There is an additional dilation associated with manually reporting the perceptual switch in Report conditions.
source: The fact that only the Report conditions show the re-dilation going well past baseline and being followed by a final constriction (significantly so for the Rivalry Report condition), suggests an additional, and later, dilation associated with manually reporting the perceptual switch.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data pattern observed in Report vs. Ignore conditions.

claim: The report-related dilation overlaps with the perception-related constriction and dampens it.
source: This dilation, although being delayed relative to the constriction, would nevertheless overlap with the constriction and dampen it, explaining the net smaller (and non-significant) initial constriction amplitude observed in Figure 2 in association with the Report conditions, as compared to the Ignore conditions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data pattern to explain the smaller constriction in Report conditions.

claim: Manual report typically follows both the perceptual event and its OKN-based concomitant by an interval that ranges between hundreds of milliseconds up to about a second.
source: These observations are consistent with the idea of a dilation component associated with the key press report, given the fact that manual report typically follows both the perceptual event and its OKN-based concomitant by an interval that ranges between hundreds of milliseconds up to about a second (Figure 1D), and therefore often happens while the perception-related constriction is still ongoing.
evidence: This is a finding from the temporal analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Both rivalry switches and on-screen switches are marked by a rapid constriction and re-dilation immediately following the switch.
source: The results of this analysis are shown in Figure 4, using the same format as Figures 2 and 3. Both rivalry switches (top plot in panels A and B) and on-screen switches (center plot in panels A and B) are marked by a rapid constriction and re-dilation immediately following the switch.
evidence: This is a finding from the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The response to on-screen switches is more rapid and pronounced than the response to rivalry switches.
source: The response to on-screen switches is, again, more rapid and pronounced, leading to a significant difference between the responses during a brief time window immediately following the switch (panel B; time axis between the top and center plot).
evidence: This is a finding from the data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Key presses are accompanied by a rapid dilation and then re-constriction back to near baseline.
source: Key presses, on the other hand, are accompanied by a qualitatively different (and also significantly different; not shown) pupil response, characterized by a rapid dilation and then re-constriction back to near baseline (bottom plot in each panel).
evidence: This is a finding from the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The biphasic pupil responses observed in Report conditions reflect a superimposition of switch-related constriction and key-press-related dilation components.
source: These results are consistent with the interpretation, articulated above, that the biphasic pupil responses (constriction, then dilation, and then return to baseline) observed in our Report conditions (Figure 2, bottom row in each panel) reflect a superimposition of these two separate components.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: A large majority of individual observers numerically show a dilation/constriction whenever a significant dilation/constriction is marked in Figure 4B.
source: Figure 4C shows per-observer data corresponding to each of the significant effects marked along the curves of Figure 4B, analogous to what Figure 3 showed in relation to Figure 2B. This again reveals a considerable level of consistency at the level of individual observers, with a large majority of individual observers numerically showing a dilation/constriction whenever a significant dilation/constriction is marked in Figure 4B.
evidence: This is an observation from the per-observer data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Authors of previous studies have observed a biphasic pupil response for reported switches that is qualitatively similar to the one found in this study.
source: Authors of previous studies have observed a biphasic pupil response for reported switches that is qualitatively similar to the one we found (Einhäuser et al., 2008; Naber et al., 2011; de Hollander et al., 2018; see also Einhäuser, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Published interpretations and analyses have tended to focus on switch-related dilation.
source: Still, published interpretations and analyses have tended to focus on switch-related dilation (probably because the dilation is generally more pronounced, with some studies reporting no constriction at all; Hupé et al., 2009; Kloosterman et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is an assessment of prior research supported by citations.

claim: Previous work has shown the net amplitude of pupil dilation following a given perceptual switch to vary with the duration of the immediately preceding perceptual dominance episode.
source: Specifically, using only conditions where perceptual switches were manually reported or otherwise task-relevant (see Discussion), previous work has shown the net amplitude of pupil dilation following a given perceptual switch to vary with the duration of the immediately preceding perceptual dominance episode (Kloosterman et al., 2015b; de Hollander et al., 2018), as well as with the duration of the immediately following one (Einhäuser et al., 2008; de Hollander et al., 2018, although see Hupé et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Previous work has shown the net amplitude of pupil dilation following a given perceptual switch to vary with the duration of the immediately following perceptual dominance episode.
source: Specifically, using only conditions where perceptual switches were manually reported or otherwise task-relevant (see Discussion), previous work has shown the net amplitude of pupil dilation following a given perceptual switch to vary with the duration of the immediately preceding perceptual dominance episode (Kloosterman et al., 2015b; de Hollander et al., 2018), as well as with the duration of the immediately following one (Einhäuser et al., 2008; de Hollander et al., 2018, although see Hupé et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research, though with some conflicting evidence noted.

claim: The finding that dilation amplitude varies with preceding dominance duration fits well with the fact that noradrenaline release in response to a given event depends on the degree of predictability of the event.
source: The former finding fits well with the fact that noradrenaline release in response to a given event depends on the degree of predictability of the event, given that an earlier end to a dominance episode is less predictable than a later one (Kloosterman et al., 2015b; de Hollander et al., 2018; see Discussion).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations to prior research.

claim: An earlier end to a dominance episode is less predictable than a later one.
source: The former finding fits well with the fact that noradrenaline release in response to a given event depends on the degree of predictability of the event, given that an earlier end to a dominance episode is less predictable than a later one (Kloosterman et al., 2015b; de Hollander et al., 2018; see Discussion).
evidence: This is based on the hazard rate of perceptual switches, supported by citations.

claim: Noradrenaline release leads to increased neural gain and altered circuit dynamics in the cortex.
source: The latter finding, in turn, is consistent with the fact that noradrenaline release leads to increased neural gain and altered circuit dynamics in the cortex (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Gilzenrat et al., 2010; Sara and Bouret, 2012), which could influence the emergence of further perceptual switches (Einhäuser et al., 2008; Sara and Bouret, 2012; Laeng et al., 2012; Kloosterman et al., 2015a; Pfeffer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Noradrenaline-related changes in cortical dynamics could influence the emergence of further perceptual switches.
source: The latter finding, in turn, is consistent with the fact that noradrenaline release leads to increased neural gain and altered circuit dynamics in the cortex (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Gilzenrat et al., 2010; Sara and Bouret, 2012), which could influence the emergence of further perceptual switches (Einhäuser et al., 2008; Sara and Bouret, 2012; Laeng et al., 2012; Kloosterman et al., 2015a; Pfeffer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Existing work has primarily treated switch-related pupil signals as noradrenaline-related dilations.
source: In other words, existing work has primarily treated switch-related pupil signals as noradrenaline-related dilations, and has aimed to fit observed relationships with perceptual dynamics into this framework.
evidence: This is an assessment of the interpretation framework used in prior research.

claim: Existing work has not attempted to separate individual components of the switch-related pupil signal.
source: However, existing work has not attempted to separate individual components of the switch-related pupil signal.
evidence: This is an assessment of the methodology used in prior research.

claim: The net dilation observed in prior work may correspond to a superimposition of both a dilation and a constriction which are shifted in time by the observer's reaction time.
source: Our above results suggest that the net dilation observed in that work may well correspond to a superimposition of both a dilation and a constriction which are shifted in time by the observer's reaction time for each report.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the current study's findings about prior research.

claim: Switch-related pupil constrictions are larger following longer dominance periods, both during rivalry and during on-screen replay.
source: Figures 5 and 6 focus on pupil responses separately per condition. For both A panels, we grouped switch events into three separate regressors, corresponding to three quantiles of the immediately preceding (Figure 5A; symbolized by the left-pointing arrow in each plot) or subsequent (Figure 6B; symbolized by the right-pointing arrow in each plot) dominance duration, from brief to long. In the former case (Figure 5A) this analysis suggests a more pronounced switch-related pupil constriction for switches that terminate a longer dominance episode, especially in the Ignore conditions (top row).
evidence: This is a finding from the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Between-switch variability in the preceding dominance duration is correlated with between-switch variability in pupil area change rate.
source: Here, we did not separate switch events into quantiles but instead included as a covariate the (normalized) durations of the perceptual dominance episodes immediately preceding the switch events. In other words, we investigated whether, at any time point within our deconvolution window, between-switch variability in the preceding dominance duration was correlated with between-switch variability in pupil area change rate.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: All four conditions show a dip in pupil area change rate shortly after the switch, consistent with a stronger constriction following longer dominance episodes.
source: Qualitatively all four plots show a dip shortly after the switch, consistent with a stronger constriction following longer dominance episodes, but this dip is significantly deeper in the Ignore conditions (time axis at the center between the four plots), and only reaches significance in those conditions, for both Rivalry and On-screen switches.
evidence: This is a finding from the data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The dip in pupil area change rate following longer dominance episodes is significantly deeper in the Ignore conditions.
source: Qualitatively all four plots show a dip shortly after the switch, consistent with a stronger constriction following longer dominance episodes, but this dip is significantly deeper in the Ignore conditions (time axis at the center between the four plots), and only reaches significance in those conditions, for both Rivalry and On-screen switches.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The correlation between preceding dominance duration and pupil area change rate only reaches significance in the Ignore conditions.
source: Qualitatively all four plots show a dip shortly after the switch, consistent with a stronger constriction following longer dominance episodes, but this dip is significantly deeper in the Ignore conditions (time axis at the center between the four plots), and only reaches significance in those conditions, for both Rivalry and On-screen switches.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There is some evidence that subsequent dominance duration is positively correlated with pupil area change rate around 2 s following the perceptual switch in the Rivalry Ignore condition.
source: Here, panel A shows only modest differences in pupil area between the three groups of perceptual switch events, now separated into quantiles of the subsequent perceptual dominance duration rather than the preceding one. Panel B is consistent with this observation. It provides some evidence that subsequent dominance duration is positively correlated with pupil area change rate around 2 s following the perceptual switch in the Rivalry Ignore condition, but statistical support for this is not quite compelling.
evidence: This is a finding from the data shown in Figure 6B, but with weak statistical support.

claim: The statistical support for the correlation between subsequent dominance duration and pupil area change rate is not quite compelling.
source: It provides some evidence that subsequent dominance duration is positively correlated with pupil area change rate around 2 s following the perceptual switch in the Rivalry Ignore condition, but statistical support for this is not quite compelling.
evidence: This is an assessment of the statistical evidence from Figure 6B.

claim: The lack of between-condition differences in the correlation with subsequent dominance duration precludes strong conclusions.
source: This lack of any between-condition differences precludes strong conclusions, both because in general terms the relevance of significant within-condition effects is predicated on the presence of between-condition differences, and because in this specific case no meaningful effect can exist in the On-screen conditions (because brain processes cannot influence the timing of on-screen events).
evidence: This is a logical inference about the interpretation of the statistical findings.

claim: No meaningful effect of pupil response on subsequent dominance duration can exist in the On-screen conditions because brain processes cannot influence the timing of on-screen events.
source: This lack of any between-condition differences precludes strong conclusions, both because in general terms the relevance of significant within-condition effects is predicated on the presence of between-condition differences, and because in this specific case no meaningful effect can exist in the On-screen conditions (because brain processes cannot influence the timing of on-screen events).
evidence: This is a logical inference about the causal relationship between pupil response and subsequent perception.

claim: The observed relation with preceding dominance duration does not reflect an artefact arising from incomplete separation of overlapping pupil responses to temporally adjacent perceptual switches.
source: A control analysis (Appendix 1—figure 7) indicates that the observed relation with preceding dominance duration (Figure 5) does not reflect an artefact arising from incomplete separation of overlapping pupil responses to temporally adjacent perceptual switches.
evidence: This is a finding from a control analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 7.

claim: What evidence exists for a relation with subsequent dominance duration might reflect an artefact from incomplete separation of overlapping pupil responses.
source: On the other hand, that same analysis suggests that what evidence we do observe for a relation with subsequent dominance duration (Figure 6) might reflect such an artefact.
evidence: This is a finding from a control analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 7.

claim: The first component of the pupil response is a rapid pupil constriction and re-dilation time-locked to the perceptual switch.
source: We used a combination of both no-report conditions and report conditions, involving both binocular rivalry and on-screen animations, to identify and decompose the switch-related pupil response into two separable components, each associated with different aspects of perceptual switches. The first component is a rapid pupil constriction and re-dilation time-locked to the perceptual switch, irrespective of whether this switch occurs during binocular rivalry or during an on-screen animation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: The first component occurs irrespective of whether the switch occurs during binocular rivalry or during an on-screen animation.
source: The first component is a rapid pupil constriction and re-dilation time-locked to the perceptual switch, irrespective of whether this switch occurs during binocular rivalry or during an on-screen animation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: The second component is a rapid pupil dilation and re-constriction time-locked to the manual response to the perceptual switch.
source: The second is a rapid pupil dilation and re-constriction time-locked to the manual response to the perceptual switch, again irrespective of the nature of the switch.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: The second component occurs irrespective of the nature of the switch.
source: The second is a rapid pupil dilation and re-constriction time-locked to the manual response to the perceptual switch, again irrespective of the nature of the switch.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: There is a robust dependence of the pupil response on the amount of time elapsed since the perceptual switch that immediately preceded the present one.
source: We found a robust dependence of the pupil response on the amount of time elapsed since the perceptual switch that immediately preceded the present one, such that switch-related pupil constrictions are larger following longer dominance periods, both during rivalry and during on-screen replay.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Switch-related pupil constrictions are larger following longer dominance periods.
source: We found a robust dependence of the pupil response on the amount of time elapsed since the perceptual switch that immediately preceded the present one, such that switch-related pupil constrictions are larger following longer dominance periods, both during rivalry and during on-screen replay.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: There is tentative evidence that the pupil response around two seconds following the perceptual switch is related to the duration of the immediately following perceptual dominance period.
source: We also found some tentative evidence that the pupil response around two seconds following the perceptual switch is related to the duration of the immediately following perceptual dominance period, but this evidence does not warrant strong conclusions.
evidence: This is a finding from the data shown in Figure 6, but with weak statistical support.

claim: The evidence for a relation between pupil response and subsequent dominance duration does not warrant strong conclusions.
source: We also found some tentative evidence that the pupil response around two seconds following the perceptual switch is related to the duration of the immediately following perceptual dominance period, but this evidence does not warrant strong conclusions.
evidence: This is an assessment of the strength of the evidence from Figure 6.

claim: The most robust finding in existing work on this topic has been of a transient pupil dilation.
source: As mentioned above, the most robust finding in existing work on this topic has been of a transient pupil dilation (Einhäuser et al., 2008; Hupé et al., 2009; Kloosterman et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is an assessment of prior research supported by citations.

claim: When switch-related pupil responses are discussed in a broader context, this is invariably in relation to dilation-linked noradrenergic modulation of cortical function.
source: Consistent with this, when switch-related pupil responses are discussed in a broader context this is invariably in relation to dilation-linked noradrenergic modulation of cortical function (Sara and Bouret, 2012; Laeng et al., 2012; Nassar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an assessment of how prior research has been interpreted, supported by citations.

claim: The transient dilation in existing work is tentatively identified with the task-related dilation in the present study.
source: In existing pupillometry studies on multistable perception, the switches were always task-relevant, so we tentatively identify the transient dilation in existing work with the task-related dilation in our present study.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current findings to prior research.

claim: The task-related dilation is, in part, related to the motor act of reporting itself.
source: Based on results from two such previous studies, we surmise that this dilation is, in part, related to the motor act of reporting itself, but is also related more generally to the task-relevance of the switch events.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior research findings.

claim: The task-related dilation is also related more generally to the task-relevance of the switch events.
source: Based on results from two such previous studies, we surmise that this dilation is, in part, related to the motor act of reporting itself, but is also related more generally to the task-relevance of the switch events.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior research findings.

claim: In two previous studies that included a condition where overt switch reports were omitted but observers needed to attend to or covertly count switches, the resulting switch-related dilations were substantially smaller than with overt report, yet not abolished.
source: Both those previous studies included a condition where overt switch reports were omitted, yet where observers did need to attend to Hupé et al., 2009 or covertly count (Kloosterman et al., 2015b) the switches. In both cases, the resulting switch-related dilations were substantially smaller than with overt report, yet not abolished, consistent with some role of task relevance per se.
evidence: This is a finding from prior research supported by citations.

claim: The task-related dilation response is an example of the pupil dilation that is generally observed in association with elevated cognitive engagement.
source: In agreement with authors of previous studies, then, we interpret our task-related dilation response as an example of the pupil dilation that is generally observed in association with elevated cognitive engagement, and that has been linked to increased activity of neuromodulatory centers including the noradrenergic locus coeruleus (de Gee et al., 2017; Laeng and Alnaes, 2019; Joshi and Gold, 2020).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Pupil dilation associated with elevated cognitive engagement has been linked to increased activity of neuromodulatory centers including the noradrenergic locus coeruleus.
source: In agreement with authors of previous studies, then, we interpret our task-related dilation response as an example of the pupil dilation that is generally observed in association with elevated cognitive engagement, and that has been linked to increased activity of neuromodulatory centers including the noradrenergic locus coeruleus (de Gee et al., 2017; Laeng and Alnaes, 2019; Joshi and Gold, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The Rivalry Ignore condition is the first to measure pupil responses to task-irrelevant perceptual switches.
source: Our Rivalry Ignore condition is, to our knowledge, the first to measure pupil responses to task-irrelevant perceptual switches, and to show that these are associated with a pupil constriction, just like switches in our On-screen Ignore condition, that is task-irrelevant on-screen switches.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the experimental approach.

claim: Task-irrelevant perceptual switches are associated with a pupil constriction.
source: Our Rivalry Ignore condition is, to our knowledge, the first to measure pupil responses to task-irrelevant perceptual switches, and to show that these are associated with a pupil constriction, just like switches in our On-screen Ignore condition, that is task-irrelevant on-screen switches.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: The pupil may constrict in response to isoluminant changes in visual input, such as changes in color, spatial frequency, or motion content.
source: We interpret these constrictions in the context of work showing that the pupil may constrict in response to isoluminant changes in visual input, such as changes in color, spatial frequency, or motion content (Barbur et al., 1992; Young et al., 1995; Conway et al., 2008; Barbur, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Constrictions in response to isoluminant input transients are similar in size, but opposite in sign, to engagement-related dilations.
source: This kind of constriction is similar in size, but opposite in sign, to the engagement-related dilation mentioned above (about 0.1 to 1 mm in diameter; Slooter and van Norren, 1980; Barbur et al., 1992; Young et al., 1993; Conway et al., 2008), matching our finding of similar magnitudes for both our positive and our negative rapid response component (but see Appendix 1—figure 6 for inter-observer differences in the relative magnitudes of the two components).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research and matches the current findings.

claim: Constrictions in response to isoluminant input transients are virtually abolished by cortical lesions.
source: Several lines of evidence suggest a cortical contribution to constrictions in response to isoluminant input transients: these constrictions are virtually abolished by cortical lesions (Barbur et al., 1992; Heywood et al., 1998), and they are modulated by attention withdrawal and interocular suppression (Kimura et al., 2014; Hu et al., 2019), as well as by stimulus properties that lack a specific representation outside of cortex (e.g. the orientation of a viewed face; Conway et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Constrictions in response to isoluminant input transients are modulated by attention withdrawal and interocular suppression.
source: Several lines of evidence suggest a cortical contribution to constrictions in response to isoluminant input transients: these constrictions are virtually abolished by cortical lesions (Barbur et al., 1992; Heywood et al., 1998), and they are modulated by attention withdrawal and interocular suppression (Kimura et al., 2014; Hu et al., 2019), as well as by stimulus properties that lack a specific representation outside of cortex (e.g. the orientation of a viewed face; Conway et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Constrictions in response to isoluminant input transients are modulated by stimulus properties that lack a specific representation outside of cortex.
source: Several lines of evidence suggest a cortical contribution to constrictions in response to isoluminant input transients: these constrictions are virtually abolished by cortical lesions (Barbur et al., 1992; Heywood et al., 1998), and they are modulated by attention withdrawal and interocular suppression (Kimura et al., 2014; Hu et al., 2019), as well as by stimulus properties that lack a specific representation outside of cortex (e.g. the orientation of a viewed face; Conway et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The most developed hypothesis for what causes constrictions to isoluminant changes is that the perturbation of visual cortical responses results in a temporary weakening of tonic inhibition of the midbrain Edinger-Westphal nucleus.
source: Indeed, the most developed hypothesis as to what causes such constrictions is that the perturbation of visual cortical responses that results from the visual input change brings about a temporary weakening of tonic inhibition of the midbrain Edinger-Westphal nucleus (Barbur et al., 1992; McDougal and Gamlin, 2008; Barbur, 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior research supported by citations.

claim: The Edinger-Westphal nucleus drives the iris sphincter muscle.
source: Since this nucleus drives the iris sphincter muscle, reducing its inhibition would lead to a smaller pupil.
evidence: This is established anatomical and physiological knowledge.

claim: Reducing inhibition of the Edinger-Westphal nucleus would lead to a smaller pupil.
source: Since this nucleus drives the iris sphincter muscle, reducing its inhibition would lead to a smaller pupil.
evidence: This is a logical inference from established physiological knowledge.

claim: The pupil response to isoluminant stimulus changes (but not the pupil light reflex) is preserved in patients with damage to the pretectal area.
source: Among several routes to the Edinger-Westphal nucleus ones involving the pretectal area have been argued not to be critical in this context, based on the observation that the pupil response to isoluminant stimulus changes (but not the pupil light reflex) is preserved in patients with damage to that area (Wilhelm et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a finding from prior research supported by a citation.

claim: One possibility is that tonic sympathetic inhibition involving the locus coeruleus is interrupted in response to visual cortical events.
source: One remaining possibility is that tonic sympathetic inhibition involving the locus coeruleus is interrupted in response to visual cortical events (Wilhelm et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by a citation.

claim: The locus coeruleus inhibits the Edinger-Westphal nucleus.
source: This option would be consistent with evidence that the locus coeruleus does inhibit the Edinger-Westphal nucleus (Wilhelm et al., 2002; McDougal and Gamlin, 2008; Mathôt, 2018; Joshi and Gold, 2020) and that it receives input from cortex (Samuels and Szabadi, 2008; Joshi and Gold, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The locus coeruleus receives input from cortex.
source: This option would be consistent with evidence that the locus coeruleus does inhibit the Edinger-Westphal nucleus (Wilhelm et al., 2002; McDougal and Gamlin, 2008; Mathôt, 2018; Joshi and Gold, 2020) and that it receives input from cortex (Samuels and Szabadi, 2008; Joshi and Gold, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Another conceivable route for pupil constriction would be via the superior colliculus.
source: Another conceivable route would be via the superior colliculus, which also has the required connectivity with both the Edinger-Westphal nucleus and cortex (Wang and Munoz, 2015; Joshi and Gold, 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: The dominant cortical input to the locus coeruleus comes from frontal cortex as well as the cingulate cortex.
source: One argument against the option involving the locus coeruleus is that the dominant cortical input to that structure comes from frontal cortex as well as the cingulate cortex (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Sara and Bouret, 2012; Joshi and Gold, 2020), whereas the present switch-related constriction seems to be associated with visual events rather than task execution and, as such, with the back of the cortex rather than the front.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Some inputs to the locus coeruleus coming from parietal and temporal cortex have been reported.
source: It should be mentioned here, however, that some inputs to the locus coeruleus coming from parietal and temporal cortex have also been reported (Samuels and Szabadi, 2008; Joshi and Gold, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The switch-related constrictions constitute a new non-invasive index of the visual cortical response change that marks perceptual switches.
source: As such, this work offers insight into the neural processes involved in perceptual switching, as well as providing a new methodological and conceptual reference point for future pupillometry work on this topic to fully deliver on its promise.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and their interpretation.

claim: If the constrictions reflect a temporary interruption of tonic sympathetic input involving the locus coeruleus, then these constrictions are a type of mirror image of the task-related dilations.
source: We note that, if it is true that these constrictions reflect a temporary interruption of tonic sympathetic input involving the locus coeruleus, then this renders these constrictions a type of mirror image of the task-related dilations we also observe, as those are thought to reflect a transient elevation of this input.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the proposed mechanism.

claim: Task-related dilations are thought to reflect a transient elevation of tonic sympathetic input involving the locus coeruleus.
source: We note that, if it is true that these constrictions reflect a temporary interruption of tonic sympathetic input involving the locus coeruleus, then this renders these constrictions a type of mirror image of the task-related dilations we also observe, as those are thought to reflect a transient elevation of this input.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about pupil dilation and noradrenaline.

claim: No existing study has shown switch-related pupil constrictions in isolation.
source: Although no existing study has shown switch-related pupil constrictions in isolation, previously-reported pupil response shapes do suggest a constriction as one constituent part.
evidence: This is an assessment of prior research.

claim: Several authors have reported task-relevant switches during perceptual multistability to be linked to a biphasic pupil response composed of an initial dip followed by a peak.
source: As mentioned above, several authors have reported task-relevant switches during perceptual multistability to be linked to a biphasic pupil response composed of an initial dip followed by a peak (Einhäuser et al., 2008; Naber et al., 2011; de Hollander et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The temporal order of the biphasic response (dip then peak) is consistent with the interpretation that prior authors have measured a combination of both rapid constriction and rapid dilation.
source: This temporal order is consistent with the interpretation that those authors have measured a combination of both our rapid constriction (which occurs first, time-locked to the switch) and our rapid dilation (which occurs later, time-locked to the report).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current findings to prior research.

claim: Reports of a biphasic response pattern have not been restricted to studies of binocular rivalry but extend to work on other forms of perceptual multistability.
source: Interestingly, reports of such a biphasic response pattern have not been restricted to studies of binocular rivalry (Naber et al., 2011; de Hollander et al., 2018) but extend to work on other forms of perceptual multistability (Einhäuser et al., 2008), suggesting that the constriction arises more generally when perception changes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The constriction arises more generally when perception changes, not just during binocular rivalry.
source: Interestingly, reports of such a biphasic response pattern have not been restricted to studies of binocular rivalry (Naber et al., 2011; de Hollander et al., 2018) but extend to work on other forms of perceptual multistability (Einhäuser et al., 2008), suggesting that the constriction arises more generally when perception changes.
evidence: This is an inference based on findings from prior research.

claim: The most prominent aspect of most published pupil response shapes is the dilation component.
source: On the other hand, the most prominent aspect of most published pupil response shapes is the dilation component, suggesting that the constriction component elicited by our particular stimulus is larger than usual.
evidence: This is an assessment of prior research and comparison to current findings.

claim: The constriction component elicited by the particular stimulus used in this study is larger than usual.
source: On the other hand, the most prominent aspect of most published pupil response shapes is the dilation component, suggesting that the constriction component elicited by our particular stimulus is larger than usual.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison to prior research.

claim: Einhäuser et al., 2008 reported that a more pronounced pupil dilation predicted a longer subsequent dominance duration.
source: Einhäuser et al., 2008, in two experiments that used multistable perception paradigms other than binocular rivalry, reported that a more pronounced pupil dilation, centered around 500 ms before the perceptual switch report in one condition, and around 500 ms after in the other, predicted a longer subsequent dominance duration, but Hupé et al., 2008 questioned that result.
evidence: This is a finding from prior research supported by a citation.

claim: Hupé et al., 2008 questioned the result that pupil dilation predicts subsequent dominance duration.
source: Einhäuser et al., 2008, in two experiments that used multistable perception paradigms other than binocular rivalry, reported that a more pronounced pupil dilation, centered around 500 ms before the perceptual switch report in one condition, and around 500 ms after in the other, predicted a longer subsequent dominance duration, but Hupé et al., 2008 questioned that result.
evidence: This is a finding from prior research supported by a citation.

claim: de Hollander et al., 2018 showed that a larger pupil during binocular rivalry predicted a longer subsequent dominance duration.
source: de Hollander et al., 2018 showed results broadly consistent with Einhäuser et al., 2008, reporting that a larger pupil during binocular rivalry predicted a longer subsequent dominance duration.
evidence: This is a finding from prior research supported by a citation.

claim: The most common interpretation of correlations with subsequent dominance duration has been that a switch-related increase of cortical noradrenaline would stabilize the newly established perceptual interpretation.
source: The most common interpretation of correlations with subsequent dominance duration has been that a switch-related increase of cortical noradrenaline, tied to pupil dilation, would stabilize the newly established perceptual interpretation, thereby delaying the next perceptual switch (Einhäuser et al., 2008; Sara and Bouret, 2012; see Kloosterman et al., 2015a for a conceptually related interpretation of different data).
evidence: This is an interpretation from prior research supported by citations.

claim: de Hollander et al., 2018 observed a correlation with preceding dominance duration: a smaller pupil shortly after the report was linked to a longer preceding dominance period.
source: de Hollander et al., 2018 also observed a correlation with preceding dominance duration: a smaller pupil shortly after the report was linked to a longer preceding dominance period.
evidence: This is a finding from prior research supported by a citation.

claim: de Hollander et al., 2018 interpreted the correlation with preceding dominance duration in terms of the hazard rate of the perceptual switch occurring.
source: Those authors interpreted that latter result in terms of the hazard rate of the perceptual switch occurring, rather than in terms of the time interval between switches as such.
evidence: This is an interpretation from prior research supported by a citation.

claim: The instantaneous probability of a perceptual switch monotonically increases as a function of time since the previous switch.
source: Specifically, given the roughly gamma-shaped distribution of perceptual dominance durations during perceptual multistability (Levelt, 1968; Borsellino et al., 1972), the instantaneous probability of a perceptual switch monotonically increases as a function of time since the previous switch.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about perceptual multistability supported by citations.

claim: de Hollander et al., 2018 argued that the relation with preceding dominance duration reflected the degree of surprise associated with the current perceptual switch.
source: Accordingly, de Hollander et al., 2018 argued that the relation with preceding dominance duration reflected the degree of surprise associated with the current perceptual switch: low surprise (following long dominance periods) was linked with a smaller pupil as compared to high surprise (following short dominance periods).
evidence: This is an interpretation from prior research supported by a citation.

claim: The interpretation of the relation with preceding dominance duration in terms of surprise is consistent with a more general body of work on surprise-linked pupil dilations mediated by noradrenaline.
source: This interpretation is consistent with a more general body of work on surprise-linked pupil dilations mediated by noradrenaline (e.g. Preuschoff et al., 2011), and also with the results of a pupillometry study that specifically manipulated the hazard rate of on-screen switches during replayed perceptual multistability (Kloosterman et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Similar to de Hollander et al., 2018, the current study found a smaller pupil (a stronger pupil constriction) shortly after switches that terminated longer dominance periods.
source: Qualitatively speaking there are similarities with the existing work: similar to de Hollander et al., 2018 we found a smaller pupil (in our case: a stronger pupil constriction) shortly after switches that terminated longer dominance periods (Figure 5) and that would, therefore, be less surprising as formalized by the hazard rate.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study's data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Consistent with both Einhäuser et al., 2008 and de Hollander et al., 2018, the current study found some anecdotal evidence that a larger pupil predicts a longer subsequent dominance period.
source: And consistent with both Einhäuser et al., 2008 and de Hollander et al., 2018, we found some anecdotal evidence that a larger pupil predicts a longer subsequent dominance period (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study's data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The main influence of preceding dominance duration is on the switch-related pupil constriction that occurs irrespective of task relevance.
source: Our data indicate that the main influence of preceding dominance duration is on the switch-related pupil constriction that occurs irrespective of task relevance.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study's data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The finding that preceding dominance duration mainly influences task-irrelevant constriction casts doubt on interpretations centered on surprise and associated noradrenaline release.
source: This casts some doubt on interpretations centered on surprise and associated noradrenaline release, notions typically related to task-relevant events and to pupil dilations.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the current findings in relation to prior interpretations.

claim: A more natural interpretation is that switch-related pupil constrictions may be subject to a type of adaptation.
source: A more natural interpretation of this aspect of our results is that switch-related pupil constrictions may be subject to a type of adaptation, either of the underlying cortical response or of a component that is closer to the iris musculature.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the current findings.

claim: Adaptation would explain why pupil constrictions are less pronounced during the time period shortly after a previous constriction.
source: Although we are not aware of any reports of adaptation affecting similar pupil constrictions in the literature, it would explain why our present pupil constrictions are less pronounced during the time period shortly after a previous constriction, as the neural process that mediates constrictions would be less responsive during that period.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed data pattern.

claim: To the extent that the pupil response predicts upcoming percept duration, it occurs in the Rivalry Ignore condition, in which switches were task-irrelevant and in which no pupil dilation was observed.
source: A related remark applies to the modest evidence, in our data, that the pupil response may predict the upcoming perceptual dominance duration. To the extent that this effect is real (but see discussion surrounding Figure 6 and Appendix 1—figure 7), it occurs in our Rivalry Ignore condition, in which switches were task-irrelevant and in which we did not observe any pupil dilation.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study's data.

claim: The finding that any prediction of upcoming percept duration occurs in the Ignore condition is not consistent with the idea that the magnitude of dilation predicts upcoming percept duration.
source: This is not consistent with the idea that the magnitude of, specifically, dilation predicts upcoming percept duration, nor with the prevailing interpretation in terms of noradrenaline release.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the current findings in relation to prior interpretations.

claim: Only in the Ignore conditions were significant correlations with preceding percept duration observed.
source: Only in the Ignore conditions did we observe significant correlations with preceding percept duration.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study's data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The data patterns observed in the Report conditions qualitatively matched those of the Ignore conditions, but showed no significant correlations with preceding percept duration.
source: The data patterns observed in the Report conditions, where switch-related constrictions and task-related dilations overlap, did qualitatively match those of the Ignore conditions, but showed no significant correlations.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study's data shown in Figure 5.

claim: One contributing factor to the lack of significant correlations in Report conditions is that the Ignore conditions had more statistical power.
source: One contributing factor here can be that the Ignore conditions had more statistical power: the correlated occurrence of both switches (linked to constriction) and key press reports (linked to dilation) in the Report conditions means that a larger amount of data is required to obtain a reliable estimate of either individual response component, as compared to the Ignore conditions in which the switches occur in isolation.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed data pattern.

claim: A control analysis does not support the alternative explanation that both switch-related constriction and response-related dilation depend on preceding percept duration in opposite directions.
source: An alternative explanation, that both switch-related constriction and response-related dilation depend on preceding percept duration yet in directions that work against each other in the combined response, is not supported by a control analysis (Appendix 1—figure 8).
evidence: This is a finding from a control analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 8.

claim: If the explanation for lack of significant correlations in Report conditions is statistical power, then that underscores the value of the no-report approach.
source: If the explanation is, indeed, to be found in statistical power, then that further underscores the value of our no-report approach to studying the pupillometric correlates of switches in multistable perception.
evidence: This is an inference about the methodological implications of the findings.

claim: The present data further strengthen the notion that the perceptual dynamics that precede a perceptual switch have an impact on its pupillary signature.
source: On the balance, our present data further strengthen the notion (Kloosterman et al., 2015b; de Hollander et al., 2018) that the perceptual dynamics that precede a perceptual switch have an impact on its pupillary signature, and add to it the finding that this impact is primarily on the switch-related pupil constriction, rather than on the task-related dilation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current findings in relation to prior research.

claim: The impact of preceding perceptual dynamics is primarily on the switch-related pupil constriction, rather than on the task-related dilation.
source: On the balance, our present data further strengthen the notion (Kloosterman et al., 2015b; de Hollander et al., 2018) that the perceptual dynamics that precede a perceptual switch have an impact on its pupillary signature, and add to it the finding that this impact is primarily on the switch-related pupil constriction, rather than on the task-related dilation.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study's data.

claim: Explanations in terms of surprise and associated noradrenaline release can, at best, account for part of the impact of preceding perceptual dynamics on pupillary signature.
source: Related, our findings suggest that explanations in terms of surprise and associated noradrenaline release can, at best, account for part of this impact, and we propose adaptation of the constriction mechanism as a possible additional explanation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the current findings.

claim: Adaptation of the constriction mechanism is proposed as a possible additional explanation for the impact of preceding perceptual dynamics.
source: Related, our findings suggest that explanations in terms of surprise and associated noradrenaline release can, at best, account for part of this impact, and we propose adaptation of the constriction mechanism as a possible additional explanation.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation proposed based on the current findings.

claim: The current findings are inconclusive regarding the idea that subsequent percept durations can be predicted from the pupil response.
source: With regard to subsequent percept duration, our findings are inconclusive regarding the idea (Einhäuser et al., 2008; de Hollander et al., 2018) that those can be predicted from the pupil response, but they form no natural fit with the notion that this would have do with switch-related noradrenaline release.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current findings in relation to prior research.

claim: The current findings form no natural fit with the notion that prediction of subsequent percept duration would have to do with switch-related noradrenaline release.
source: With regard to subsequent percept duration, our findings are inconclusive regarding the idea (Einhäuser et al., 2008; de Hollander et al., 2018) that those can be predicted from the pupil response, but they form no natural fit with the notion that this would have do with switch-related noradrenaline release.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the current findings.

claim: There is a tendency for the pupil to dilate shortly before the switch in the Rivalry conditions, and not in the On-screen conditions.
source: But our plots (Figures 2 and 4) also appear to show a tendency for the pupil to dilate shortly before the switch in the Rivalry conditions, and not in the On-screen conditions.
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: The pre-switch dilation tendency did not reach the chosen significance level of alpha=0.01.
source: We did not center our interpretations on this tendency because its significance level does not quite reach our chosen alpha of 0.01 in our analyses.
evidence: This is a statistical assessment of the data.

claim: A pre-switch dilation, if real, would be consistent with measurements in other experimental domains that suggest elevated cognitive engagement around the time of perceptual switches during perceptual multistability.
source: Such a pre-switch dilation, if real, would be consistent with measurements in other experimental domains that suggest elevated cognitive engagement around the time of perceptual switches during perceptual multistability, even as compared to on-screen replay conditions (e.g. frontoparietal fMRI BOLD signals, Lumer et al., 1998; various EEG markers, Kornmeier and Bach, 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The data seem to show a stronger pre-stimulus dilation in the Rivalry Report condition than in the Rivalry Ignore condition.
source: and the fact that our data seem to show a stronger pre-stimulus dilation in the Rivalry Report condition than in the Rivalry Ignore condition (Figure 2) could be seen as evidence for a role in translating the perceptual experience into a behavioral response.
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The OKN-based algorithm appears to overestimate the number of switches for slow switchers, and to underestimate it for fast switchers.
source: Nonetheless, our algorithm appears to overestimate the number of switches for slow switchers, and to underestimate it for fast switches (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A control analysis argues against the possibility that the OKN-based algorithm specifically tends to miss switches that are closely spaced in time.
source: One possibility is that the OKN-based algorithm specifically tends to miss switches that are closely spaced in time, but a control analysis argues against that possibility (Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from a control analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 4.

claim: The OKN-based algorithm may have both a non-zero, and fixed, false alarm rate, and also a hit rate that is lower than 100%.
source: Our OKN-based algorithm may have both a non-zero, and fixed, false alarm rate (i.e. a certain number of spurious switch events is marked per unit time), and also a hit rate that is lower than 100% (i.e. a certain proportion of actual switches is not marked).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed data pattern.
